To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the chronic administration of opioids produces an irreversible (or very slowly reversible) defect of the Ca2+- and calmodulin-dependent protein kinase system in the rat striatum.

chronic morphine treatment decreases the level of phosphorylated proteins in rat striatal synaptic membranes, and this change can be mimicked by the addition of Ca2+-free buffer to the protein kinase assay, but not by the addition of calmodulin to the protein kinase reaction.
chronic morphine treatment of animals decreases the level of phosphorylated proteins in the rat striatum and this decrease is not reversed by the addition of Ca2+ and calmodulin to the assay.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of calmodulins in the opioid receptor-coupled phosphorylation of striatal synaptic membrane.
the effects of chronic morphine on the phosphorylation of synaptic proteins of the striatal membrane.
the biochemical mechanisms of tolerance and dependence to opioids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the opioid receptors in the brain are coupled to a G-protein which in turn is coupled to a Ca2+-cal-modulin dependent protein kinase system which is responsible for the regulation of the phosphorylation of synaptic proteins.
the opioid receptor system is a major modulator of the phosphorylation state of proteins in the brain.
the chronic administration of opiates produces a change in the Ca2+ dependent protein kinase system of brain membranes which is not due to the loss or absence of calmodulin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic morphine treatment of the rat decreases the level of phosphorylated proteins in the striatal synaptic membrane.

chronic morphine treatment of the rat decreases the phosphorylation of striatal synaptic membrane and synaptosomal proteins, and this decrease is not restored by the addition of exogenous Ca2+ and calmodulin.

opioids produce a long-lasting decrease in the level of phosphorylated proteins, and that the decrease in the phosphorylation is not due to a decrease in Ca2+ levels or to a decrease in the level or function of calmodulin, the Ca2+-binding protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
chronic opioid use leads to changes in the phosphorylating ability of the brain, which may be a contributing factor in the development of tolerance to the analgesic and rewarding effects of opioids.
the chronic use of morphine leads to changes in the protein kinase system of the brain, and these changes are likely to be involved in the tolerance and withdrawal phenomena.
the opioid receptor system is intimately linked to the regulation of protein phosphorylation in the brain.
